anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Excessive or poorly-written application statements and transaction demarcations that drive the engine to touch more rows, return larger result sets, or keep transactions open longer than the true business need.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Exhaustion of kernel-enforced objects such as file handles, shared-memory segments, semaphores, threads, or cgroup quotas, preventing the database process from acquiring the operating-system resources it requests.

When these two root causes strike simultaneously, users observe an extreme long-tail of statement latencies, frequent timeouts, and sporadic "cannot allocate resource" or "too many open files" errors. Queries that already scan or lock large data ranges because of sub-optimal SQL now stall mid-execution when the engine cannot obtain additional file descriptors, worker threads, or shared memory. Connection storms triggered by application-level retries further deplete process or thread quotas, leading to partial outages where existing sessions hang in uninterruptible I/O or lock-wait states while new sessions are refused. Monitoring shows CPU and I/O utilisation well below capacity, yet wait-time histograms are dominated by OS-level resource acquisition waits and user-level lock/latch contention amplified by the prolonged transactions.

Causally, poorly tuned SQL inflates the demand for kernel resources—longer scans keep file handles, buffers, locks, and threads alive, while batched or Cartesian operations require more temporary files and memory mappings. This pushes the database process toward the fixed OS limits faster than anticipated. Once limits are hit, the kernel denies new allocations, which in turn causes the database to pause or retry internal operations, lengthening execution time and holding application locks even longer. The extended lock holds and session backlogs feed a positive feedback loop, aggravating both the workload-logic inefficiency and the OS resource scarcity, eventually cascading into widespread performance degradation and intermittent service outages.

entry.official_description: This member is configured with a group_replication_paxos_single_leader option value of 1 and it is trying to join a group with Communication Protocol Version below 8.0.27. In order to join this group, group_replication_paxos_single_leader value must be configured to the value 0. This member will now exit the group.
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with connection establishment, authentication exchange, protocol correctness, network reachability, or client/server communication stability.
entry.solution_guidance: Check endpoint reachability, authentication flow, connection limits, protocol compatibility, transport stability, and client connection lifecycle management.
